title: 'V-Effect' Explodes in Popularity.. Key Chains and Baseball Caps Worn by BTS's V See Prices Double Amid 'Sold Out Again and Again' - starnewskorea.com
content:
Products worn by BTS's V triggered consecutive sell-outs, clearly demonstrating the "V-effect." During his performances in Toronto, Canada, on August 22–23, V wore a CN Tower maple leaf key chain and a Canadian flag baseball cap, sparking sell-outs. Fans shared information about store inventory and purchase locations, while the price of the baseball caps surged from $17 to $35, more than doubling. BTS held their "World Tour Arirang" concert at Toronto's Rogers Stadium on August 22–23. During this performance, V wore a key chain shaped like the maple leaf of Toronto's landmark CN Tower and a baseball cap featuring the Canadian flag. A fan who visited the CN Tower to purchase the key chain reported that all items were already sold out and they could not confirm when restocks would occur. The fan stated, "Staff members also said they didn't know when more key chains would be restocked and wondered why so many people were seeking this product. Once I told them V used it, they understood." The baseball caps worn by V also sold out at all stores. Fans attempting to buy the caps began sharing purchase location information, saying, "They are already completely sold out, and wholesalers also have no inventory in stock." Even after the price of these caps rose from $17 to $35, they remained sold out everywhere. title: Former CR-V Owner Slapped With $815 Bill For SUV He Sold 15 Years Ago - Carscoops
content:
The Honda's buyer never transferred the Honda into his name, leaving its former owner with a very expensive blast from the past Selling a used car usually means pocketing the cash, waving goodbye and forgetting about it. But for Toronto resident Mario Iamundo, a 2002 Honda CR-V he sold way back in 2011 recently returned to his life in the least welcome way possible: as a four-figure bill. Iamundo received a CA$1,130 ($815) charge this summer from Classic Towing and Storage in Etobicoke for towing and storing the Honda SUV. The problem was that although he’d sold the CR-V 15 years earlier and its status had been marked as sold, the buyer apparently never completed the ownership transfer. Related: Kia EV Owner Adds $2 Of Electricity, Gets A Bill For $16,000 That meant Iamundo remained the last registered owner, though he wasn’t the vehicle’s actual owner. “I was responsible to pay the storage fees for a car I haven’t seen in 15 years, which doesn’t seem fair to me,” he told CTV News. Whether anyone had actually been driving the old Honda during its decade-and-a-half away from Iamundo isn’t known. Classic Towing and Storage general manager Kevin Araya told CTV that used-car buyers failing to transfer registrations happens more often than you might expect. His advice for private sellers is to not hand over the keys until the buyer has changed the ownership into their name. Ontario gives used-car buyers six days after a sale to register themselves as the new owner. Once that deadline passes, sellers can visit ServiceOntario and have the vehicle’s status changed to sold. But that doesn’t transfer the registration. If the buyer doesn’t complete their side, the seller can remain listed as the last registered owner. That’ll sound familiar to some Americans, although certain states give sellers an extra layer of protection. In California, for example, sellers must notify the DMV within five days using a Notice of Transfer and Release of Liability. The buyer still has to complete the ownership transfer, but filing the notice generally shifts responsibility for subsequent parking and traffic violations and civil liability to them. Texas has a similar safety net. Sellers can file a Vehicle Transfer Notification, which adds the sale to the state’s vehicle record. Filing it within 30 days can protect the seller from liability even if the buyer fails to transfer the title promptly. And in the UK, the seller gets the buyer to fill in their details on the registration document at the point of sale, and sends it off themselves to make sure the ownership transfer is logged. Iamundo ultimately – and very reluctantly – paid the CA$1,130. But he believes consumers deserve better protection from bills arriving years after a sale. His experience with a CR-V that he thought had left his life years ago certainly makes a compelling case for closing Ontario’s paperwork gap. title: Days After GTA 6's Big Reveal, Rockstar Announces A Major GTA 5 Update - Polygon.com
content: Grand Theft Auto 5 will introduce a revamped world with better NPCs Grand Theft Auto 6 may be around the corner, but don't count out Grand Theft Auto 5 just yet. Rockstar announced Tuesday that GTA 5 will soon receive a roleplay-focused update called nopixel V. It'll transform the base game into a multiplayer experience where fans can tell their own stories. Coming up with your own ideas has always been possible, but nopixel adds bespoke roleplaying options to the mix. Rockstar is promising a reworked character customization system that will help players tell unique stories. The world is also upgraded: better visuals and smarter, more reactive NPCs. nopixel will offer more ways to make money, whether you want to play as a hardened criminal or a law-abiding citizen. The update introduces new areas, like a grand hotel-casino and a revamped version of Cypress Flats. Those are the new bits, but Rockstar says there's a lot more to come. According to a Rockstar blog post, GTA 5 will eventually receive other improvements, such as a new PC game overlay, more events, and "expanded access" to nopixel. The post reads, "Every player helps shape the city, and every relationship matters." The closed beta for nopixel begins on Sept. 8 and will be available straight out of the Rockstar Games Launcher. "GTA Roleplay has never felt more alive, and there has never been a better time to tune in," Rockstar says. There's still no official word on how GTA 6 will incorporate GTA Online's role-playing elements, or even when the game is coming to PC at all. Until the open-world sequel comes out, nopixel might be the closest thing fans can get to experiencing GTA 6's in-depth NPC system. title: Queen Máxima, Princess Amalia and the Royals confirmed to attend Harald V’s funeral: Who will be there - HOLA
content: Queen Máxima and Princess Amalia will travel to Norway to join members of Europe’s royal families in bidding a final farewell to King Harald V. All eyes are now on the Royal Palace in Oslo, where mourners have gathered to pay their respects to the late monarch after his 35-year reign. Norway is tightening security ahead of Harald V’s state funeral on September 9 at Oslo Cathedral, where Queen Máxima and Princess Amalia will be joined by King Willem-Alexander, Princess Beatrix and other European royals. Norwegian authorities are preparing what they have described as the largest security operation in the country’s history as royal families and prominent world leaders travel to Oslo for the ceremony. The Norwegian Royal Court announced Harald V’s death on August 28, automatically making Crown Prince Haakon King Haakon VIII and marking the beginning of a new chapter for the monarchy. The death of a king carries a bittersweet reality for his successor: mourning the loss of a father while simultaneously assuming the throne. It also sets in motion an elaborate series of ceremonies and protocols intended to honor a monarch at the end of a historic reign. Norway is now preparing to welcome some of the world’s most prominent dignitaries, including King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark. Following the announcement of the state funeral, the Danish royal couple postponed their state visit to Belgium, originally scheduled for September 8, to a date yet to be determined. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium later confirmed that they, too, would travel to Norway. The royal reunion that had been expected to take place amid glittering tiaras and evening gowns will instead happen under far more somber circumstances, as Europe’s royals gather to mourn Harald V. The Danish delegation, however, has not yet been finalized. According to the official statement, the attendance of additional members of the Danish royal family will be confirmed in the coming days. It therefore remains unclear whether Queen Margrethe or other members of the family will attend the ceremony. Japan, meanwhile, will be represented by Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko. The couple will travel to Norway to pay their respects to Harald V, father of the current King Haakon VIII. According to local media reports, extensive security preparations are also underway for the possible attendance of U.S. President Donald Trump. Following the solemn state funeral at Oslo Cathedral on September 9 and the final farewells from royal families around the world, Harald V will be laid to rest in a private burial. His final resting place will be the Royal Mausoleum at Akershus Fortress, the landmark medieval stronghold overlooking the fjord in the Norwegian capital. There, in the royal crypt, Harald V will rest alongside his parents, King Olav V and Princess Märtha, and his grandparents, King Haakon VII and Queen Maud. Surrounded by his closest family and accompanied by a 21-gun salute, the private ceremony will bring Norway’s farewell to Harald V to a close. It will also mark the formal end of his 35-year reign and the beginning of a new era under King Haakon VIII. © ¡HOLA! title: Ariana Grande Introduces Swarovski Classica 2026 - V Magazine
content: Across 29 calla lily-inspired pieces, Classica brings Swarovski’s brilliance to a closer scale, with Ariana Grande demonstrating its versatility Across 29 calla lily-inspired pieces, Classica brings Swarovski’s brilliance to a closer scale, with Ariana Grande demonstrating its versatility Jewelry made for daily wear is judged differently from a piece chosen for one highly visible moment since it has to remain interesting after the first impression and comfortable enough to be reached for again. For Swarovski, a house whose identity has long been tied to the visual impact of crystal, Classica offers a way to explore that balance at a closer and more personal scale. Introduced in September 2026, the 29-piece collection includes pendants, bracelets, rings, and earrings designed to sit comfortably against the body, whether worn individually or layered in different combinations. The pieces share curved lines and interlocking shapes that connect the collection visually while preserving the uniqueness of each design. Global Creative Director Giovanna Engelbert begins with the calla lily, focusing on the flower’s long curve and balanced proportions instead of reproducing it as a recognizable floral motif. She translates those qualities into rounded forms and softly structured silhouettes, creating jewelry that reflects the flower’s natural movement without copying its appearance. Those curved forms are crafted from sterling silver sourced from recycled materials, with certain pieces offered in an 18K gold finish and Swarovski Zirconia set in pavé or used as individual accents. The combination of softer silhouettes and precise stone placement makes the jewelry suitable for regular wear while giving each piece enough definition to remain visible on its own. Classica’s emphasis on versatility also supports Swarovski’s wider LuxIgnite strategy, which aims to expand the house’s jewelry portfolio across more occasions and styles of dressing. The collection adds a more restrained option to the catalog without moving away from the technical detail and focused use of light associated with Swarovski. The campaign makes that versatility visible through Ariana Grande, who appears as the house’s global brand ambassador in images conceived by Engelbert and photographed by longtime collaborators Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott. title: Ahead of GTA 6, Rockstar Games Reveals Its Official GTA Online Roleplaying Server nopixel V - ign.com
content: Rockstar Games has revealed its official GTA Online roleplaying server, nopixel V, ahead of GTA 6's launch. Grand Theft Auto 5 is one of the most popular games of all time, and part of that is thanks to major community support. In the late 2010s and early 2020s, modders went particularly crazy with the foundation Rockstar created and utilized it for roleplaying servers, such as the extremely popular nopixel. Rockstar has embraced this side of the community, acquiring the team behind the FiveM modding platform and collaborating with nopixel itself. Now, nopixel is gearing up to release the next iteration of its roleplaying server, which will be officially supported by Rockstar Games. The two teamed up to produce a much richer and deeper roleplaying experience that will feature a reworked character customization system, enhanced graphics, and a wealth of quality of life changes. Perhaps the most notable thing for longtime GTA fans is that the Mile High Club, a building that has been under construction since the game's very first reveal trailer in 2011, has been finished exclusively for nopixel. The building is now a hotel and casino for roleplayers. The server will be available directly through Rockstar's official launcher, meaning you won't have to tinker with any third-party tools or platforms, and players will be able to see it in action on September 8 when a bunch of the top RP streamers will be let loose on the streets of Los Santos. You can click here to check out a trailer, which showcases the depth and uniqueness of this new GTA experience. Of course, many fans are likely going to wonder what this means for GTA 6. Rockstar Games has yet to make any kind of comments or announcement on the next iteration of GTA Online, but it would be shocking if there wasn't an online mode for GTA 6 later down the line. The single-player of GTA 6 is already a very roleplay-intensive experience, so it seems like Rockstar may be designing the game with a roleplay future in mind. Whether nopixel will have its own GTA 6 RP server remains to be seen, but it would be surprising if Rockstar abandoned this side of the game when entering the next era. If this is just the beginning of a long term collaboration, GTA 6's online could be extremely special. Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris is honoured to announce its patronage of the Paris Opera for the 2026/2027 season. More than a philanthropic initiative, this partnership embodies a meaningful dialogue between two iconic institutions united by a shared dedication to excellence, transmission, craftsmanship and emotion. Together, they celebrate the talents and artistic traditions that enrich Paris's cultural landscape and inspire audiences from around the world. Throughout the 2026/2027 season, selected guests of Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris will enjoy reserved seating and privileged opportunities to experience the Paris Opera from a unique perspective, offering exceptional access to an institution at the very heart of Parisian cultural life. In turn, Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris will welcome members of the Paris Opera community for stays and special occasions, providing a setting where artists, creators and professionals can gather, exchange ideas and continue to nurture artistic expression. This spirit of reciprocity resonates naturally between two institutions driven by the same pursuit of beauty, excellence and emotion. Behind the grandeur of every performance, much like behind the seamless experience of a stay at George V, lies the dedication of countless talented individuals whose expertise transforms vision into reality and creates unforgettable moments. On one side are singers, musicians, dancers, artisans and technicians whose collective talents bring each production to life. On the other are chefs, sommeliers, florists, artisans and hospitality professionals who shape every guest experience. In both worlds, excellence is a collective achievement, where every detail matters and every gesture reflects extraordinary precision, passion and savoir-faire. title: Dale V. Kinch Obituary - mitchellfuneral.com
content: Dale Vaughn Kinch, age 93, of Jackson, Michigan, passed away on August 29, 2026, leaving behind a remarkable legacy of family, education, community service and a well lived life. Dale was born on December 26, 1932, to Russell and Beatrice (VanAntwerp) Kinch in Jackson, Michigan. A lifelong learner he dedicated much of his life to educating, mentoring, and encouraging others. He graduated from Jackson High School in 1951. Dale graduated from Albion College, and later graduated from Eastern Michigan University with a double Master’s Degree in Arts and Administration. Dale served as an educator for Michigan Center High School for 38 years, touching the lives of generations of students. His influence extended well beyond the classroom. Dale was not only a teacher, but he also served as the men’s basketball coach, wrestling coach, and the women’s cheerleading coach. He was a mentor whose influence remained with his students long after graduation. After his retirement, Dale continued to serve Michigan Center Schools volunteering his time helping to raise money for charities. His motto was “People helping people.” Dale was a member of the Michigan Center Rotary Club. He was also a member of the Jackson Eagles 612, Michigan Center Eagles 3634, as well as White Cloud Eagles. Dale is preceded in death by his parents, Russell and Beatrice Kinch. He is survived by his wife, Clarene (Treadway-Palmer) Kinch of 15 years. He is also survived by his daughters, DeeDee DuBose (Will Scott), Danielle (Kirk) Ford; his step- son James (Ruby) Chifane; his grandchildren: Stephen (Megan) Shelden-Ford, Dusti Gleason, Derricka Gleason, Emma Ford, Connor DuBose and Carson DuBose. He also has 10 great-grandchildren. Dale had a genuine curiosity about the world. He enjoyed traveling and camping. He was an avid reader and had a passion for family genealogy, enjoyed learning and studying U.S. Presidents, as well as Michigan History. Dale also enjoyed playing bingo, and singing in the choir at Arbor North Semi-Assisted Living Center, where he has resided for the past 14 years. Anyone who Dale knows he enjoyed U of M football and had a love for the Detroit Tigers, never missing a game. Dale spent a lifetime teaching lessons, and his influence will continue for generations to come. His lessons will be remembered, his laughter will be missed, and his smile will never be forgotten. Funeral services will be held at the Caskey-Mitchell Funeral Home on Saturday, September 5, 2026, at 2:00 p.m., where the family will receive friends from 1:00 - 2:00 p.m. A private burial will be held at Pleasant Grove Cemetery. title: Richard V Licata Obituary - Orange County Register
content: Richard Vincent Licata passed away peacefully on August 2, 2026, in Vancouver, Washington, after a 3-year battle with prostate cancer. He was 73. Rick was born on December 28, 1952, in Montebello, CA, to Vincent and Lucille Licata. He attended Foothill High School in Tustin and graduated from Cal State Fullerton with a BA in Business Administration in 1976. That same year, Rick married Connie Childs, with whom he had two daughters, Kathy and Rebecca. Rick’s father owned a chain of health food stores, and Rick had planned to take over the business when he felt called to vocational ministry. He and his family moved to Massachusetts to attend Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, where he graduated with a Master of Divinity degree. Rick taught at Calvary Chapel Bible School in Twin Peaks, California for 2 years, before taking a position as an associate pastor at a Calvary Chapel in Vancouver, where he served for several years. He took positions at churches in Vancouver, British Columbia, and Wieser, Idaho before returning to Vancouver, Washington, where he started a new church that, within 2 years, had grown to more than 200 people. When his first marriage ended, Rick left pastoral ministry. He then married Paula Zarzana, and they adopted three children, Alex, Soren, and Elizabeth. Over the next several years, he continued to teach bible studies at several churches. In his last year, he took the head pastorate of Kenton Presbyterian Church in Portland, Oregon. He continued to preach sermons until he became physically incapable of continuing a few months before his death. Rick is survived by his children: Kathy Young, Rebecca Baer, granddaughter Joanna, Alex, Soren, and Elizabeth Licata, and his brothers Frank, Vince, Tom, and Jim Licata. title: 5 Reasons You Need a 2026 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing In Your Life - autoguide.com
content: As General Motors phases out the spectacular Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing, 2026 marks its final year of production in its current iteration. Among the crowd of homogenized luxury vehicles, the Blackwing stands as a beacon of fire, lightning, and brutalist thunder. It isn't just a world-class super-sedan—it's arguably the best-driving four-door production car on the planet and a forever car for any true enthusiast. If you're considering putting one in your garage before it disappears into the history books, here are 5 reasons why you need the 2026 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing in your life: At the heart of the Blackwing lies the legendary supercharged 6.2-liter LT4 V8. Pumping out a thumping 668 horsepower and 659 lb-ft of torque, this engine delivers instant, unrelenting throttle response via an Eaton blower. In a landscape dominated by turbocharged engines with noticeable lag, the LT4’s power delivery feels like a glory-days racing engine. Available with your choice of a Tremec six-speed manual or a 10-speed automatic transmission, it delivers an involving excitement that rival all-wheel-drive sedans simply cannot replicate. Tipping the scales right around 4,100 pounds, the CT5-V Blackwing is remarkably light for its class. That relatively light weight pays massive dividends in the corners. The chassis feedback, communicative steering, and stopping power are almost otherworldly. For those seeking the absolute pinnacle of performance, the optional $18,000 Precision Package adds increased spring rates, a larger front stabilizer bar, recalibrated MagneRide dampers, an eLSD, and carbon-ceramic brakes—making it a world-class track titan. Despite its unhinged capabilities on open or twisty roads, the Blackwing's visual design is remarkably restrained. Unless outfitted with aggressive carbon fiber aero packages, its angular bodywork looks more like a dignified luxury sedan than a 668-horsepower track monster. Save for large exhaust tips and subtle functional vents, it doesn’t flaunt its power. It’s the ultimate sleeper sedan: those who know, know—allowing you to fly comfortably under the radar until you choose to let the demon under the hood run free. The interior prioritizes high functionality without overcomplicating the driver's experience. Dominated by a massive 33-inch LED color touchscreen angled toward the driver, the infotainment system is fast, intuitive, and pleasant to use. It offers standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility, a standard Performance Data Recorder (PDR) for track days, and standard SuperCruise hands-free driving tech for highway cruising. Up front, luxury amenities like heated, ventilated, and massaging seats make long trips effortless. Twenty-two years after Cadillac debuted the CTS-V to challenge the BMW M5, the CT5-V Blackwing stands as the pinnacle of that performance lineage. While competitors like the M5, Audi RS 7, and Porsche Panamera have transitioned toward heavier, coddling hybrid setups, the rear-wheel-drive Blackwing remains the last pure, raw gas-powered super-sedan on sale today. content: par Max Grünwald | 28 août 2026 | Monde de l'aviation, Histoire et légendes | 0 commentaire On 6 August 1969, a Soviet helicopter lifted 40,204.5 kilograms — just over 40 tonnes — to a height of 2,255 metres. That is roughly the weight of a loaded articulated lorry, carried straight up by rotors. No helicopter has lifted more, before or since. The aircraft that did it was the Mil V-12, and it is the largest helicopter ever built by a margin that nothing has come close to challenging in fifty-seven years. Taper: Mil V-12 (production designation Mi-12, NATO: Homer) — heavy-lift helicopter Mise en page: Two five-blade rotors side by side on inverse-taper wings, cross-shafted Diamètre du rotor : 35.0 m each; span across the rotor tips about 67 m — wider than a Boeing 747 Moteurs : Four Soloviev D-25VF turboshafts, roughly 6,500 shp each Weights: Empty about 69,100 kg; maximum take-off 105,000 kg Construit: Two, both of which flew; both wore the registration CCCP-21142 Enregistrer: 40,204.5 kg lifted to 2,255 m on 6 August 1969 — never surpassed Survivants : One at the Mil plant at Panki-Tomilino, one at the Central Air Force Museum, Monino Mil studied the obvious options first. A single main rotor big enough to lift twenty-five tonnes runs into blade and gearbox limits that were not solvable in the 1960s. A tandem layout like the Chinook's does not scale gracefully to that weight either. The transverse layout solved a different problem: it let Mil take two complete rotor, gearbox and engine assemblies from the existing Mi-6 — a proven, in-service system — and mount one at each wingtip. That is an enormous reduction in development risk. It also disposed of the tail rotor, which on a large single-rotor helicopter absorbs power for no lift at all. The rotors overlap by about three metres and are cross-shafted, so they stay synchronised and so the aircraft stays controllable if an engine fails. The port rotor turns anticlockwise and the starboard clockwise, putting the advancing blades inboard. The stubby wings are inverse-tapered — wider at the tip than the root — to sit under the downwash without blanking it. The first flight attempt, on 27 June 1967, ended badly: a control feedback oscillation built up and the aircraft made a hard landing that burst a tyre and bent a wheel hub. Western press reports at the time claimed it had been destroyed. It had not. The first successful flight came on 10 July 1968, from Panki to Lyubertsy, with Vasily Koloshenko at the controls. A second prototype followed in 1973. Those two were the entire production run. Mustard’s film on the V-12 — nearly three million views, and the clearest account of why the layout was chosen. The V-12 flew to the Paris Air Show at Le Bourget in 1971, stopping at Groningen on the way, and was, predictably, the largest thing there. It won the Sikorsky Prize. Mikhail Mil himself never saw it — he had died in January 1970. The V-12 existed for one reason: to carry the components of intercontinental ballistic missiles to launch sites in parts of the Soviet Union with no roads and no railways. Its cargo hold was sized around that job — 28 metres long and 4.4 metres square. Then the requirement evaporated. Solid-fuelled ICBMs on road and rail mobile launchers no longer needed to be flown to remote fixed sites, and reconnaissance satellites had made the concealment argument moot anyway. The air force declined to put the aircraft through state acceptance trials. The Mi-6 and Mi-10 could handle everything the military actually needed lifting, and nothing in the civil economy could justify the running costs. The programme stopped in 1974. A planned Mi-12M with more powerful engines never got past a mock-up. One point of care, because it is widely misreported. Many sources — including Russian-language ones and parts of Wikipedia's own prose — give the payload as 44,205 kg. The FAI's record file and Wikipedia's specification table both give 40,204.5 kg. Use the lower figure. A second point: it is accurate to say no helicopter has ever lifted more. It is not accurate to say the record still stands as a current FAI record, because the FAI has since retired or superseded those particular categories in a rules change. The achievement is untouched; the paperwork has moved on. And a sanity check worth making, since the numbers get quoted loosely: 69,100 kg empty plus a 40-tonne payload comes to more than the 105,000 kg maximum take-off weight, before fuel. The record flight was an overload attempt. Normal cabin payload was around 25 tonnes. Period Soviet footage of the V-12 flying — worth watching for the sheer implausibility of it leaving the ground. Two were built. Neither entered service. One record was set, and it has outlasted the country that set it. Somewhere at Panki-Tomilino, the first one is still sitting outside — the largest helicopter anyone has ever managed to fly, built for a job that stopped existing before it was finished. title: Genalo v. G.M. - American Civil Liberties Union
content: In 2024, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled that Keisy G.M., a lawful permanent resident who had been subjected to mandatory detention for 21 months, could not be detained any longer without a hearing on whether he poses a flight risk or danger. That decision was consistent with the vast majority of federal court rulings on the government’s practice of detaining people for prolonged periods of time without any individual hearings. The Trump administration appealed the ruling in January 2026 and on June 15 the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, setting oral argument for Oct. 13, 2026. The Trump administration is taking a radical position the government has not taken in the 30 years since this mandatory detention statute, 8 U.S.C. 1226(c), was enacted by Congress. It says immigrants like Mr. G.M. do not have a protected liberty interest in not being locked up without a hearing — at a time when the administration is pushing hard to detain and deport as many immigrants as possible, often locking people away in inhumane ICE detention centers, where deaths are already at record levels. On the government’s theory, it can lock up people under this mandatory detention statute for months, years, or even decades, without a hearing — as long as the removal case is still ongoing. The American Civil Liberties Union, New York Civil Liberties Union, MacArthur Justice Center, and Hecker Fink LLP are co-counsel. The groups argue the federal appeals court ruling is correct, and that the Constitution protects all of us, regardless of immigration status, from being locked away without due process. (Ole Berg-Rusten/Pool Photo via AP) OSLO, Norway (AP) — The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title. Harald passed away Friday at age 89, and his son, the crown prince, immediately became King Haakon VIII. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Haakon, 53, will take the oath to Norway’s constitution on Tuesday. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. Mette-Marit has been largely absent from the public eye in the wake of her lung transplant in June. She was diagnosed in 2018 with pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive disease that damages and scars lung tissue. It can cause serious breathing problems, and there is no known cure. Mette-Marit and Queen Sonja, Harald’s widow, held hands and walked behind the coffin during Monday’s procession. Since Harald’s death, the royal family and the country have been in an official state of mourning. Norwegians and visitors expressed their grief over the weekend by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. The coffin stayed in the palace’s Red Salon over the weekend before traveling to the royal chapel on Monday, where it will remain until the funeral. title: The “born free and equal” clauses and Lawrence v. Texas - SCOTUSblog
content: This is the third of seven introductory articles on the relevance for constitutional law of the “born free and equal” clauses, which appeared in the Declaration of Independence and in six out of 12 state constitutions when the federal Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791, and in 24 out of 37 state constitutions when the 14th Amendment was ratified in 1868. The “born free and equal” clause of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, for example, provided that: In my first two articles, I showed that the “born free and equal” idea is deeply rooted in American history and tradition as that phrase is used in such correctly decided cases as Washington v. Glucksberg (the right to assisted suicide is not deeply rooted in American history and tradition), McDonald v. City of Chicago (the Second Amendment’s right to own a handgun for self-protection extends to the states because it is deeply rooted in American history and tradition), and Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (the right to an abortion is not deeply rooted in American history and tradition). In this third introductory article, I want to examine the application of the “born free and equal” clauses to another famous “right to privacy” case: 2003’s Lawrence v. Texas, which struck down so-called “sodomy” laws banning oral and anal sex as unconstitutional. In my last article, I explained why: 1) there is no such thing as a constitutional “right to privacy” of the kind found incorrectly in Roe v. Wade, yet 2) why the outcome in Griswold v. Connecticut, the pivotal 1965 case striking down laws banning the use of contraceptives, is nonetheless correct under the privileges or immunities clause, which applied the “born and free and equal” clauses as modified by Corfield v. Coryell (discussed below) to the states. I’ll apply this analysis to Lawrence v. Texas to explain why I think that case was rightly decided but not for the reasons given by Justice Anthony Kennedy in his opinion for the court. To back up a bit, the seminal case of Corfield v. Coryell, decided in 1823, was dispositive as to the original meaning of the privileges or immunities clause of the 14th Amendment according to the framers of that amendment. In Corfield, Justice Bushrod Washington explained: Note that the language in italics makes clear that the 14th Amendment protects only rights deeply rooted in history and tradition. The language in bold face is a paraphrase of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780’s “born free and equal” clause and is a privilege or immunity of citizens of the United States. At the same time, the underlined passage critically limits the “born-free-and-equal” idea by making all rights “subject nevertheless to such restraints as the government may justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” This language marks the origin of what we today call the rational basis test (and what the Lochner-era Supreme Court wrongly called a reasonableness test). In Lawrence v. Texas, the Supreme Court struck down as unconstitutional a Texas sodomy law that applied only to gay and lesbian couples. The court said in dicta that sodomy laws applying to heterosexual couples also violated the Constitution. It did so based on the so-called “right to privacy” found in Griswold v. Connecticut. Since I argued in my last article that there is no such right, I turn now to whether the decision in Lawrence v. Texas was correct under the “born free and equal” clauses and the privileges or immunities clause of the 14th Amendment as discussed above and in my two prior articles. The first question is whether a right to commit so-called “sodomy,” either by heterosexual or gay and lesbian couples, is deeply rooted in our nation’s history and tradition; that is, whether this is part of the “born-free-and-equal” idea that everyone has the right “to enjoy life and liberty” and to “pursue and obtain happiness and safety.” While the right to commit sodomy has long been criminalized, freedom among committed adult couples to enjoy sexual relationships in every way is arguably covered by the deeply rooted rights to “enjoy liberty” and to “pursue and obtain happiness and safety.” This question then becomes what is the correct level of generality at which to analyze this issue. Sodomy laws, while of ancient vintage, have almost never been enforced in modern times, except against gay and lesbian people. Although all 50 states and the District of Columbia had such laws in 1960, by 2003, when Lawrence v. Texas was decided, 37 out of the 50 states had repealed their sodomy laws, and these laws were almost never enforced by the 13 states which retained them in 2003. Indeed, the only way to get prosecuted for sodomy in 2003 in the 13 states that retained such laws was to call the police to come to your house during the commission of such an act (which is exactly what happened in Lawrence). Under these circumstances, one must remember Judge Robert H. Bork’s prophetic words in “The Tempting of America: The Political Seduction of the Law,” in which Bork, one of the founding fathers of modern originalism, stated that: “The world changes in which unchanging values [I would say ‘legal texts’] find their application.” This is a profound observation for an originalist. It means that originalists must not only look at the original public meaning of a text when it is adopted: they must also apply that text to a modern world which presents new technologies and changed circumstances such that the constitutional text must be translated to apply to them. Translation occurs, for example, when we apply the First Amendment’s protection of freedom of speech and of the press to expressive conduct like flag burning, or to hand-written material in a private diary, or in a private letter to a friend, or in broadcast movies, radio, television, and the internet where freedom of expression is constitutionally protected even in the absence of speech – a vocal utterance – or in the absence of a “printing” press. In “The Tempting of America,” Bork had no trouble finding that the 14th Amendment’s overarching commitment to racial equality, relied upon in Brown v. Board of Education, trumped the original expected application of many of the 14th Amendment’s framers who mistakenly said in congressional debates, in 1868, that racial equality was somehow consistent with segregated public schools and anti-miscegenation laws. This was clearly not true by 1954, as to public schools, and by 1967, as to anti-miscegenation laws.The Supreme Court was therefore right to hold that public school segregation and anti-miscegenation laws are unconstitutional in the modern world even though many of the members of Congress who voted for the 14th Amendment said otherwise. Exactly the same thing holds true with respect to sodomy laws in 2003. In 1868, the framers of the 14th Amendment, when they wrote Corfield v. Coryell’s version of the “born free and equal” right (subject to a rational basis test) into the privileges or immunities clause of the 14th Amendment, mistakenly thought that sodomy laws were somehow consistent with the “born-free-and-equal” idea. As late as 1986’s Bowers v. Hardwick, a 5-4 majority of the Supreme Court agreed. But by 2003, with only 13 states having sodomy laws on the books, which they almost never enforced, and decades after the birth control pill was legalized on May 9, 1960, which helped launch a sexual revolution, the rise of the modern feminist movement, and the gay rights movement, it became as difficult to square sodomy laws with the “born-free-and-equal” command of the privileges or immunities clause as it was to square segregated public schools and laws banning inter-racial marriage with the “no race discrimination” command of the 14th Amendment. Thus, when Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954, or when Loving v. Virginia was decided in 1967, or when Lawrence v. Texas was decided in 2003, it was not enough to rely on original expected applications of the framers of the 14th Amendment, which, in fact, undercut the 14th Amendment’s central textual rights. In other words, an originalist judge cannot let constitutional rights – even open-ended rights – be overridden by a clearly mistaken, original expected application of the relevant text. This still leaves open the key question of whether sodomy laws should have been upheld in 2003 under the rational basis test. As noted earlier, that test also originates in Justice Washington’s Corfield v. Coryell opinion, which states that the rights to “enjoy liberty” and to “pursue and obtain happiness and safety” are “subject nevertheless to such restraints as the government may justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” Were sodomy laws in 2003, or today in 2026, then “justly prescribed for the general good of the whole [people]”? The answer is “no” for the reasons given by Justice Byron White in his concurrence in Griswold v. Connecticut. There is a lack of means-ends fit to sodomy laws: they intrude on a highly personal sexual liberty right for the dubious purpose of promoting only sex that could lead to childbirth. Yet in a world where contraceptive use is almost universal (even among Catholics, whose church still formally prohibits it), isolating out the act of sodomy for punishment makes little sense. One could just as plausibly punish non-procreative sex by couples using birth control, by heterosexual couples where the woman is post-menopausal, or even masturbation, by individual men and women. All these activities are sexual acts that do not lead to the possibility of childbirth. Is there any rational basis for criminalizing sodomy but not such other conduct? The answer is “no.” Punishing the non-procreative sexual acts of gays and lesbians is especially unfair to such persons given they have no control over who they are attracted to. As my friend Akhil Reed Amar has argued many times on this site, the citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment, along with the “born free and equal” clauses, commands birthright equality, regardless of whether one is born gay or straight. For this reason, the 13 mostly unenforced state sodomy laws on the books flunk the rational basis test. While I think Lawrence v. Texas thus reached the right outcome in holding sodomy laws to be irrational and unconstitutional, I believe Justice Anthony Kennedy’s majority opinion is vacuous, for many of the reasons pointed out by Justice Antonin Scalia in his dissent. As Scalia made clear, Kennedy’s majority opinion appears to write John Stuart Mills’ harm principal from “On Liberty” (that one’s actions should only by limited so much as they do harm to others) into the 14th Amendment, which is just as wrong as writing Herbert Spencer’s “Social Statics” into that amendment as the court did in the infamous case of Lochner v. New York striking down as unconstitutional perfectly valid laws establishing maximum working hours. To be clear: Among the many laws that I think rationally trump an individual’s right to “enjoy liberty” and “pursue and obtain happiness and safety” are laws criminalizing: 1) polyamory, 2) prostitution, 3) incest, 4) suicide, and 5) the use of dangerous drugs and narcotics regulated by the government. As Scalia once told me, and as I entirely agree, the people who are disproportionately “harmed” by all six of the activities listed above are women, children, and the elderly who are among the most vulnerable members of society. Laws banning these six activities, and probably many others, are then subject “to such restraints as the government may justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” The six criminal laws listed above easily pass the rational basis test, unlike laws against sodomy but which ban no other forms of non-procreative sex. Americans, and the Constitution, have always opted for a regime of “ordered liberty” and not for constitutionalizing John Stuart Mill’s harm test. In my next column, I will analyze through the lens of the “born free and equal” clause the Supreme Court’s gay and lesbian marriage opinion in Obergefell v. Hodges, in which it found a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law. title: Track by Track: V Torres – Woman - The Indy Review
content:
LA-based singer/songwriter V Torres captivated me with the first three singles from her upcoming album Woman. The title track, “Winter Solstice” and “That Night” showcased her vibrant and roots mix of indie rock and Americana. Torres describes her new album as “a journey” and a “testament on things that have shaped the woman I am today.” With the album dropping tomorrow, September 1st, Torres gave us a track-by-track breakdown of every song on the album, which you can read below! The idea behind beginnings started with the concept that every ending leads to a new beginning and every beginning will have an ending. It’s the cycle of life. The thought that everything is temporary. Something that has become somewhat of a mantra for me. It also focuses on how hard it is when you feel ready to love someone, but they are not ready to receive that love. It’s that tender moment of realizing that everyone’s timing is different and their own. The song encourages evolving and strengthening the relationship with yourself, as that is the one that needs to be looked at before you can look at relationships with others. How can we change if we always stay the same? When writing this song, I went through iterations of how the rhythm of the guitar would end up before settling on the staccato beat of the track. I think it lends itself to an interesting way for the vocal melody to dance around the guitars in the verses. I also wanted to add an 808 to the beginning of the bridge so that the listener could really feel the shift and the weight of the song opening up. I really love how the bridge builds into the breakdown chorus. Fun fact about this song is that it was not originally slated for the record. I sent my co-producer my demo of it and he insisted that it belonged on the record. I am so glad we included it. This is the title track of the record. “Woman” is my song for Women that really steps into the journey of being a Woman and being inspired by Women. The constant grind women experience, and often-times, the attending to the needs of others, while trying to keep it all together.  The grief we experience in letting go of the past versions of ourselves and the roles we play: lover, mother, caretaker, friend, etc. There is still a hopefulness somewhere in the journey and strength and acceptance of life and the work we have to do to heal. The light we see in this is the letting our guard down and being open again to love. When I first wrote the song, I wanted the acoustic guitar and drums to drive the rhythm of the song. It feels as though you are riding horseback through the desert. My lead guitarist, Kira Lingman, added her lead lines to bring a Latin/americana feeling to the track. Making the music video for Woman was really fun. Cinematographer, Dylan Pelle, approached me and said he wanted to make a desert themed music video and that he thought my music would lend well to it. We listened to all the songs on the record, and it was clear that Woman was the track to use. It already has a cinematic feeling to it, and we wanted to capture that old spaghetti western vibe. We shot in the Joshua Tree desert, at an old grimy motel in Rosemond, and at an abandoned music venue in Hermosa Beach. It was a lot of fun to see our vision come to life. This is a track I wrote when a very close friend of mine had lost her brother to a tragic accident. I was in a position of wanting to console and be there for them but there really was nothing I could do for them at the time. These words came out fast and the song was written on the Winter Solstice, hence the name. This friend is one of those people who makes everyone feel loved and good. They are always the one making everyone laugh. They had been there for me through really hard times, and this song was written for them during this time. Sometimes you don’t have the words to express what you want to say. Sometimes the act of just giving someone a silent hug is enough. I wanted this song to embody that feeling of being there for someone who’s always there for everyone else and I think in some part of this it was also giving myself that love. Knowing that you can love someone from afar and you can love yourself and hold yourself up even when you’re feeling alone. Visually, the Winter Solstice is the darkest night of the year, but it also leads to more light coming through in the near future. I felt like the visual of that dark night was present in this song but the sliver of light on the horizon was a sign of hope and something to look forward to as well. Sonically, I heard the harmonies of the chorus in my head when I was writing the song. I wanted it to start a little more rocking and surf/punk like but then turn into this beautiful choir during the chorus lines. I also wanted a slide guitar in the song to give it a little bit more americana and that tinge of country. When I hear the slide guitar, it feels like a hug, it feels like comfort and can bring me to tears, which is exactly what this song is really all about to me. This song is about the possibilities of a new adventure and allowing yourself to be open to vulnerability. It paints a picture of the moment when you go from being friends with someone to falling for them and seeing them in a completely different way. It’s highlighting that scary and exciting part of letting your guard down. The song sits in the anticipation of letting go and letting them know how you feel. Lingering in that moment when there isn’t an answer yet can be exciting to think of the potential that life has ahead for you. Sonically, I wanted those intro harmonies to shine and cut through. I really love how the song is a little more stripped down during the verses and a little more dance-y than the rest of the tracks. The guitar line I play after the first verse was inspired by the sound of the Breeders and it’s one of my favorite parts of the song along with the vocal intensity of chorus that comes after the bridge. The ending speaking part in the song is my grandmother speaking the bridge line in Spanish. I wanted her to be a part of this record and had her send me a voice note to include in the song. True story, I went to Joshua Tree for the first time and stayed in an air bnb on a property that got raided by the police in search of the body of a woman who had gone missing weeks prior. Yes, it’s crazy and yes, it happened. This moment was scary and tragic, and it got me thinking about how finite life is. I started thinking about my own life and that I wasn’t living my most authentic self. It got me thinking about what is “right” and what is “wrong” and what is the grey area in life. Can we live in that area? Being raised catholic was a lot of things but the whole “sinning” part of life and not being able to express your true self without it being thought of as unconventional or just plain wrong was running through my head. This song explores a desert landscape where there is no right or wrong, just the grey. I love how this song is more of a harder rock song than the rest of the record. I added a harmony in the chorus that I feel brings a little psychedelic rock into the song. I really love the bridge of the song that takes the song on a segue into a really cool, stripped-down groove. My lead guitarist, Kira Lingman, wrote that bridge line on the guitar and we really ran with it from a production standpoint to create this interesting breakdown which includes me using the WAH pedal for the first time on a record. The production feeling on the bridge makes me feel like something BECK would have done. This is probably the oldest song I wrote for this record. I was going through my divorce about 9 years ago. My ex called me and asked if I knew what today was. Thinking, thinking, I had no idea what he was talking about. He said it was six months to the day since we split. I had heard someone earlier in one of my yoga classes say that time was just a man-made thing. That thought came right back up to me when I realized I was not tracking this time period like he was. I immediately started writing Great Escape. The song is about leaving a situation that is not right for you anymore. It is both the knowing what you did was the right thing but also the challenges with loneliness in the aftermath. You need someone to console you and tell you everything will be okay, but you do not have that person to do so. When I wrote the song, I really wanted it to have variations in timing and melodies. I knew that I wanted the song to start with a faster tempo that felt driving and I wanted the chorus to be in half time. I felt like the half time chorus really spoke to the message of the song and symbolized the feeling of time and processing the emotion of the track. Conversely, I wanted the bridge of the song to feel like you were running through the middle of the night frantically searching for some kind of sign that you are going to be okay. I wanted it to feel chaotic and uncontrolled. The BPM of the song changes from 119 to 151. If you listen to the beginning of the song right after the end of the song, it seems SO slow, but it works in context of the song from start to finish. It was challenging recording the song and understanding where it sat the best tempo-wise. At one point I suggested a slower tempo from the offset, and it was exactly what the track needed to really get to the right place. It’s sludgy, beautiful and electric how it all turned out. I feel like it’s the most epic song on the record. This song is about getting older and knowing less. Realizing that so many thoughts and influences go into your decisions as a younger person and the older you become, the more you realize that you really don’t need to think that hard.  It is also about opening up myself to loving again after patterns of running away. Sonically, I had a demo of this track that I gave to my co-producer, and it was really bare boned with just guitar and vocals. We almost wanted to keep the demo version because there was something really beautiful and vulnerable that was perfect about it. We opted into re-recording it through amp splitting with a ‘72 Princeton reverb and a Roland jazz chorus. I was really pleased with how the guitar tones and vocals shine through on this short and sweet track. Pre-Save the album here (or starting tomorrow, play it wherever you stream music). title: Norwegians line up at memorials remembering the late King Harald V; funeral set for Sept. 9 - MPR News
content: Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Tens of thousands of Norwegians lined up Sunday in front of cathedrals and churches across the country for memorial services held for the late King Harald V, who died at 89. Harald passed away Friday and his son immediately became the new King Haakon VIII. Since Harald’s death, the royal family and the country have been in an official state of mourning. Norway’s royal palace said Sunday evening the funeral will take place on Wednesday, Sept. 9. Mourners expressed their grief over the weekend by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. “This Sunday is different. His Majesty King Harald is dead. A family has lost their spouse, father, grandfather, father-in-law,” said Dean Pål Kristian Balstad as he opened a memorial service in Oslo Cathedral, Norway's public broadcaster NRK reported. MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. The royal family attended a service at Asker Church, southwest of Oslo. Some Norwegians decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported. Harald’s son, the new king, eulogized Harald on Saturday night. He expressed his pain over the death of his beloved father and promised to lead the country with the same dedication. “I’m going to miss him. I’ll miss his laughter. His good-natured way of dealing with people and situations,” Haakon said in his first speech as new king that was broadcast live on public television. Trying to hold back his tears, he vowed to give everything for the country as its king. “That means — in the ultimate sense — being willing to risk everything, even one’s life, for Norway’s freedom and independence,” Haakon said. The new king adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. Norway’s monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity status and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world. At the time of his death, Harald was Europe’s oldest monarch. The popular king modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who have abdicated in recent times. Harald was born in 1937 in Asker, near Oslo, becoming the first Norwegian prince to be born in the country since King Olav IV in 1370. In the following centuries, Norway didn't have a king of its own until Harald's grandfather, Haakon VII, was elected king following the 1905 dissolution of the union between Sweden and Norway. Harald was 3 years old when the Nazis occupied Norway at the start of World War II. To avoid capture, his mother fled with him and his sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, first to Sweden and then by boat to the U.S., while Harald’s father and grandfather went into exile in Britain with Norway’s government. During their time in the U.S., the Norwegian royals were often guests at the White House. Harald was 6 when he carried out his first official duty, christening new warplanes at a Norwegian air base in Canada. The family was reunited in Norway in June 1945, shortly after the end of the war in Europe. Harald attended public schools, the Norwegian military college and Oxford University. Like his father — an Olympic champion sailor in 1928 — Harald loved the sea and sailboats. He represented Norway at several Olympics, and in 1987 he skippered his yacht to gold in the World Championships. As a young man, Harald was urged to find a bride among Europe's noblewomen and princesses. For nine years he shunned a series of prospects, holding out until he finally won his father’s permission to marry his longtime sweetheart, Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a successful businessman. King Olav had feared the marriage would weaken Norway’s still-young monarchy. Instead, Norwegians greeted the Aug. 29, 1968, wedding with jubilation, and later embraced Sonja as their queen. The couple had two children, Haakon and his older sister, Märtha Louise. The Norwegian Constitution was altered in 1990 to allow the first born, regardless of gender, to take precedence in the line of succession. However, it was not applied retroactively, meaning that Haakon continued to take precedence over his sister. When Harald assumed the throne on Jan. 21, 1991, he adopted the same motto his father and grandfather had used: “All for Norway.” He spent the next years trying to modernize the monarchy. “It has been my experience that the monarchy stands strong,” he once said. “This is not least because my father and grandfather did most things right. That puts me under pressure, but I take it as a challenge.” Harald won the praise of the country with an emotional speech at a memorial service after a right-wing extremist, Anders Behring Breivik, killed 77 people in bomb and gun attacks in Norway in 2011. “I remain convinced that the belief in freedom is stronger than fear. I remain convinced in the belief of an open Norwegian democracy and society. I remain convinced in the belief in our ability to live freely and safely in our own country," the king said. In 2016, Harald gave an unexpected and impassioned speech in support of LGBTQ+ equality, refugees and religious tolerance, saying “Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other.” He added that many Norwegians have emigrated from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Poland and other countries and that they “believe in God, Allah, the universe and nothing.” The public speech extolled the diversity of the Scandinavian nation and was viewed on social media by millions. Scandal and serious allegations have hung over the Norwegian royal family this year. Harald’s daughter-in-law, now-Queen Mette-Marit, faced renewed scrutiny over her connections with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. That raised questions over her judgment, though she is not accused of any wrongdoing. Mette-Marit apologized for the situation she put the royal family in, part of a broader apology for all those she had “disappointed.” At around the same time, her eldest son, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted of rape in a high-profile trial and sentenced to four years in prison. Høiby, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship before she met Haakon, has no royal titles or official duties. In 2022, Harald’s daughter Princess Märtha Louise gave up royal duties after raising eyebrows by saying she could communicate with angels and becoming engaged to an American man who identifies as a shaman. They married two years later. In January 2024, after the abdication of Denmark’s Queen Margrethe — his second cousin — Harald said that he stood by the oath he made when ascending the throne: “It lasts for life.” However, he was hospitalized twice on foreign trips after that, including during a 2024 vacation in Malaysia when he was fitted with a pacemaker and during a February 2026 holiday on the Spanish island of Tenerife when he had a skin infection. The death of King Harald resonated in Minnesota, too — where many people had a brush with the royal family over the years. Harald made several trips to the Midwest — most recently in 2011, when he and Queen Sonja visited Duluth to rededicate Enger Tower. On that trip, they also stopped in the Twin Cities and at St. Olaf College, as well as Luther College in Iowa. Now-King Haakon was still crown prince when he was in Minnesota last fall, making stops in the Twin Cities and at St. Olaf in Northfield. Haakon visited Norway House in Minneapolis and met with Gov.
